topic: Word Swap (Verbal Ability and Reading Comprehension)

sections.title: Advanced Concept of Level 3 Word Swap
sections.content: In Level 3 Word Swap questions, multiple words in the same sentence may be placed incorrectly. Usually, two separate swaps are required (such as A ↔ C and B ↔ D). The words are often placed in collocations that appear correct at first glance, but deeper analysis reveals that they do not match the context or logical meaning of the sentence.

sections.title: Multiple Swap Detection
sections.content: Step 1: Carefully read the entire sentence and understand the main idea. Step 2: Identify the key words (nouns, adjectives, verbs). Step 3: Detect which words appear to be misplaced based on meaning. Step 4: Identify two possible swaps. Step 5: After making both swaps, read the sentence again and check whether the meaning and logical flow are completely correct.

sections.title: Deceptive Collocation Analysis
sections.content: Step 1: Identify collocations (such as strong argument or heavy rain). Step 2: Check whether the word is normally used with that noun or verb. Step 3: If the collocation seems unusual, the word may belong to another part of the sentence. Step 4: Create the correct collocation through swapping and verify the logical meaning of the sentence.

sections.title: Critical Reasoning Check
sections.content: Step 1: Identify logical relationships such as cause-effect, comparison, or contrast in the sentence. Step 2: Detect the word that breaks this logical relationship. Step 3: Examine the position of words with similar or opposite meanings. Step 4: Confirm that the logical relationship becomes correct after the swap.

sections.title: Editorial Sentence Complexity
sections.content: Step 1: Divide the sentence into smaller clauses. Step 2: Understand the meaning of each clause separately. Step 3: Identify incorrect collocations or contextual mismatches. Step 4: Perform two or more swaps to reconstruct the correct meaning. Step 5: Finally, check the overall tone and logical flow of the entire sentence.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content: 1. Assuming only one swap is required when two swaps may be necessary. 2. Ignoring subtle collocation errors. 3. Not understanding the full context of the sentence. 4. Failing to recheck the sentence after performing swaps.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: Level 3 Word Swap questions involve multiple swaps, deceptive collocations, and deeper contextual analysis. To solve them correctly, it is important to carefully examine the structure, meaning, and logical flow of the entire sentence.

tricks.title: Two-Pair Swap Trick
tricks.explanation: If a single swap does not fully correct the sentence, look for another possible swap.
tricks.example: Many questions involve A ↔ C and B ↔ D type swaps.

tricks.title: Collocation Check Trick
tricks.explanation: Check whether the adjective or verb naturally fits with the noun.
tricks.example: Strong tea is correct, while powerful tea sounds unusual.

tricks.title: Clause-by-Clause Analysis
tricks.explanation: Break the sentence into smaller parts and analyze each clause separately.
tricks.example: First understand the main clause, then examine the subordinate clause.

tricks.title: Meaning Consistency Trick
tricks.explanation: After swapping, ensure that the entire sentence expresses a consistent idea.
tricks.example: The cause and effect relationship should remain clear.

tricks.title: Hidden Error Detection
tricks.explanation: Identify words that seem correct at first but actually contradict the deeper meaning.
tricks.example: Words like 'decline' may conflict with contexts such as economic growth.

tricks.title: Pair Matching Trick
tricks.explanation: Sometimes identifying logical word pairs helps detect the incorrect placements.
tricks.example: Words like risk and safety may belong to different parts of the sentence.

tricks.title: Final Flow Check
tricks.explanation: Read the entire sentence normally after all swaps are done.
tricks.example: If the sentence reads naturally like an editorial line, the solution is likely correct.

tricks.title: Elimination with Logic
tricks.explanation: Ignore the collocations that clearly appear correct and focus on the doubtful ones.
tricks.example: Mark the correct pairs first and then locate the incorrect pairs.
